q: Which city is the capital of Australia?
fact: Canberra was purpose-built as a compromise between rivals Sydney and Melbourne, to a design by American architects Walter Burley Griffin and Marion Mahony Griffin.

q: Which strait separates Spain from Morocco?
fact: At its narrowest point Europe and Africa are only about 14 km apart, close enough to see across on a clear day.

q: Which capital city is built across 14 islands where Lake Mälaren meets the Baltic Sea?
fact: Its metro is nicknamed the world's longest art gallery, with artworks decorating about 90 of its 100 stations.

q: Which great river has no bridges across its main channel?
fact: Its mouth is so wide that it holds Marajó, an island roughly the size of Switzerland.

q: Which mountain range is traditionally seen as the boundary between Europe and Asia?
fact: The range runs for about 2,500 km, from the Arctic coast down to Kazakhstan.

q: Which is the smallest country in the world by area?
fact: At under half a square kilometre, it is only about a third of the size of London's Hyde Park.

q: Which city is the capital of Canada?
fact: Queen Victoria chose Ottawa as the capital in 1857, partly as a compromise between English- and French-speaking regions.

q: Mount Kilimanjaro, Africa's highest mountain, is in which country?
fact: Kilimanjaro is a dormant volcano made up of three volcanic cones: Kibo, Mawenzi and Shira.

q: Which country has the world's only non-rectangular national flag?
fact: Nepal's constitution includes step-by-step geometric instructions for drawing the flag correctly.

q: Which river flows through the centre of Paris?
fact: The banks of the Seine in Paris are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

q: Which river flows through Vienna, Bratislava, Budapest and Belgrade?
fact: Its basin is shared by 19 countries, making it the most international river basin in the world.

q: Which is the northernmost capital city of a sovereign state?
fact: Most of its homes are heated with natural hot water from geothermal sources.

q: Which is the largest hot desert in the world?
fact: Covering around 9 million square km, it is almost as big as the United States.

q: Most of the Atacama, the driest non-polar desert on Earth, lies in which country?
fact: NASA has tested Mars rovers there because its dry soil is so similar to the Martian surface.

q: Which country is the world's fourth-largest island?
fact: Around 90% of its plants and animals, including its famous lemurs, evolved there and are found naturally nowhere else.

q: Which is the deepest lake in the world?
fact: It holds around a fifth of all the unfrozen fresh surface water on the planet.

q: Which city is the capital of Turkey?
fact: Ankara became the capital in 1923, even though Istanbul is far larger and straddles Europe and Asia.

q: The Panama Canal links the Pacific Ocean with which other ocean?
fact: Thanks to Panama's S-shape, the canal's Pacific entrance actually lies further east than its Atlantic one.

q: Mount Everest sits on the border between Nepal and which other country?
fact: It was named after surveyor George Everest, who reportedly objected to the honour.

q: Which is the largest country in Africa by area?
fact: Algeria took the title in 2011, when South Sudan became independent and Sudan's area shrank.

q: Which city is the capital of New Zealand?
fact: Wellington is the southernmost capital city of any sovereign state.

q: Which city is the capital of Brazil?
fact: Built from scratch and opened in 1960, its city plan resembles an aeroplane or bird when seen from above.

q: In which US state is the Grand Canyon?
fact: The canyon was carved over millions of years by the Colorado River.

q: Which South American country is named after the imaginary line that runs through it?
fact: Thanks to Earth's bulge, the summit of its Chimborazo volcano is the point farthest from Earth's centre.

q: Lake Titicaca lies on the border between Peru and which country?
fact: The Uros people live on floating islands they build from totora reeds.

q: Which tiny Pyrenean country is ruled jointly by two co-princes?
fact: Its official language is Catalan, rather than Spanish or French.

q: Christopher Cockerell tested his idea with a cat food tin, a coffee tin and a vacuum cleaner. What did he invent?
fact: The first full-size hovercraft crossed the Channel on 25 July 1959, 50 years to the day after Blériot's flight.

q: Which word did Alexander Graham Bell suggest for answering the telephone?
fact: Thomas Edison is credited with popularising 'hello' instead.

q: Which locomotive won the Rainhill Trials in 1829?
fact: Built by George and Robert Stephenson, it reached a top speed of about 30 mph.

q: In which year did the Mayflower sail from Plymouth to North America?
fact: Before the famous voyage, she was a cargo ship that had spent many years in the wine trade.

q: During the Great Fire of London in 1666, what did Samuel Pepys bury in his garden?
fact: His diary was written in shorthand and was not deciphered and published until the 1820s.

q: Ernő Rubik invented his famous cube in 1974. Which country was he from?
fact: It took Rubik more than a month to solve his own puzzle for the first time.

q: The Crystal Palace was built in Hyde Park for which event?
fact: Its designer, Joseph Paxton, was inspired by the ribbed leaves of a giant water lily.

q: Who was the first woman to fly solo across the Atlantic, in 1932?
fact: She landed in a farmer's field in Northern Ireland rather than her planned destination of Paris.

q: Which Wonder of the Ancient World stood at Alexandria in Egypt?
fact: Known as the Pharos, it gave its name to the word for lighthouse in several languages, such as French 'phare'.

q: Which explorer reached the east coast of Australia aboard HMS Endeavour in 1770?
fact: To get his wary sailors to eat sauerkraut, Cook had it served at the officers' table so the crew would want it too.

q: Ferdinand Magellan's expedition of 1519–1522 was the first to do what?
options: Find the source of the Nile
fact: Of the five ships that set out, only one, the Victoria, made it home.

q: Who invented the World Wide Web in 1989?
fact: His boss at CERN scribbled 'vague but exciting' on the original proposal.

q: Which civilisation built Machu Picchu?
fact: Built in the 15th century, it was little known to the outside world until 1911.

q: What did the Romans call London?
fact: The city was founded around AD 47, just a few years after the Roman invasion of Britain.

q: Which Roman emperor ordered a wall to be built from the River Tyne to the Solway Firth?
fact: The wall stretched about 73 miles (117 km) from coast to coast.

q: Whose tomb did Howard Carter discover in the Valley of the Kings in 1922?
fact: Tutankhamun became pharaoh when he was only about nine years old.

q: Which emperor, the first to rule a unified China, was buried with the Terracotta Army?
fact: The Terracotta Army was discovered in 1974 by farmers digging a well.

q: Where did the Wright brothers make their first powered aeroplane flight in 1903?
fact: That first flight lasted just 12 seconds and covered about 120 feet (37 metres).

q: The Rosetta Stone was the key to decoding which writing system?
fact: It carries the same decree in three scripts: hieroglyphic, Demotic and Ancient Greek.

q: Who led the first expedition to reach the South Pole, in 1911?
fact: His team relied on sled dogs and Inuit-style fur clothing to cope with the cold.

q: Which British monarch reigned for 63 years, a record later passed by Elizabeth II?
fact: Her children married into royal families across Europe, earning her the nickname 'grandmother of Europe'.

q: What was the name of the ship on which Charles Darwin sailed around the world?
fact: The voyage was planned to last two years but took almost five, from 1831 to 1836.

q: Who introduced printing with movable metal type to Europe around 1440?
fact: Fewer than 50 copies of the famous Gutenberg Bible are known to survive today.

q: Which civilisation built the city of Tenochtitlan on an island in a lake?
fact: Mexico City now stands on the same site, much of it on the drained lake bed.

q: Which Norse explorer reached North America around the year 1000?
fact: The remains of a Norse settlement at L'Anse aux Meadows in Newfoundland prove the Vikings got there.

q: Who reached the summit of Everest with Tenzing Norgay in 1953?
fact: News of their success reached London on the morning of Queen Elizabeth II's coronation.

q: Marie Curie was the first woman to win which famous award?
fact: She won Nobel Prizes in two different sciences: physics in 1903 and chemistry in 1911.

q: The world's first underground railway opened in 1863 in which city?
fact: Its first trains were pulled by steam locomotives.

q: What was the name of the ancient network of trade routes linking China with the Mediterranean?
fact: Despite the name, it carried far more than silk, including spices, glass, horses and the secret of paper-making.

q: The Bayeux Tapestry tells the story of the Norman Conquest of England in which year?
fact: Despite its name, it is embroidered rather than woven, so it isn't technically a tapestry.

q: Which English king agreed to Magna Carta in 1215?
fact: It was sealed at Runnymede, a meadow beside the River Thames in Surrey.

q: What is the chemical symbol for gold?
fact: Gold is so malleable that a single gram can be beaten into a sheet covering more than half a square metre.

q: Which gas do plants take in from the air to make their food?
fact: The oxygen plants release during photosynthesis comes from splitting water molecules, not from the carbon dioxide.

q: How many bones are there in an adult human body?
fact: Babies are born with around 300 bones, but many of them fuse together as they grow.

q: In which part of the body is the stapes, the smallest bone?
fact: The stapes is roughly the size of a grain of rice, and its name is Latin for 'stirrup', which it resembles.

q: Which element has the chemical symbol K?
fact: The K comes from 'kalium', a word traced back to the Arabic for plant ashes, where potassium compounds were first found.

q: Which scientist developed the theory of general relativity?
fact: Satellite navigation has to correct for relativity, or GPS positions would drift by roughly 10 km every day.

q: What is the hardest natural substance on Earth?
fact: Diamond and graphite, the 'lead' in pencils, are both made of pure carbon, just with the atoms arranged differently.

q: Which organ in the human body produces insulin?
fact: The first person ever treated with insulin was 14-year-old Leonard Thompson, in Toronto in January 1922.

q: Which temperature scale starts at absolute zero?
fact: William Thomson became a Glasgow professor at 22 and later took the title Lord Kelvin from the river beside the university.

q: Which gas makes up most of the Earth's atmosphere?
fact: Argon makes up almost 1% of the air, and its name comes from the Greek for 'lazy' because it barely reacts with anything.

q: Roughly how fast does light travel in a vacuum?
fact: Sunlight takes about 8 minutes and 20 seconds to travel from the Sun to the Earth.

q: Who discovered penicillin in 1928?
fact: Fleming spotted mould killing bacteria on a culture dish that had been left out while he was away on holiday.

q: Which element did Marie Curie name after her home country?
fact: Her laboratory notebooks are still radioactive and are kept in lead-lined boxes at France's national library in Paris.

q: Which element was detected in the Sun before it was found on Earth?
fact: It showed up as a mysterious yellow line in sunlight during an 1868 eclipse, but wasn't isolated on Earth until 1895.

q: What is the largest organ of the human body?
fact: As well as protecting you, your skin makes vitamin D when it is exposed to sunlight.

q: In DNA, which base always pairs with adenine?
fact: If you unravelled the DNA from just one of your cells and laid it end to end, it would stretch about 2 metres.

q: Which blood type is known as the universal donor for red blood cells?
fact: Austrian scientist Karl Landsteiner discovered the ABO blood groups in 1901 and later won a Nobel Prize for it.

q: Scurvy is caused by a lack of which vitamin?
fact: Royal Navy sailors were given lime juice to prevent scurvy, which is how British sailors got the nickname 'limeys'.

q: Which element has the atomic number 1?
fact: Hydrogen makes up roughly three-quarters of all the ordinary matter in the universe by mass.

q: What is the pH of pure water at 25°C?
fact: The pH scale was introduced in 1909 by Danish chemist Søren Sørensen while working at the Carlsberg brewery's laboratory.

q: Which metal is a liquid at room temperature?
fact: Another metal, gallium, melts at about 30°C, so a piece of it will turn liquid if you hold it in your hand.

q: How many chambers does the human heart have?
fact: An adult heart beats roughly 100,000 times a day, pumping blood around the whole body.

q: Which scientist wrote the Principia, setting out the laws of motion?
fact: Newton later ran the Royal Mint, where he personally investigated counterfeiters.

q: The microwave oven was invented after what melted in an engineer's pocket?
fact: The first food Percy Spencer deliberately cooked with microwaves was popcorn.

q: Which subatomic particle carries a negative electric charge?
fact: J.J. Thomson discovered the electron in 1897 at the Cavendish Laboratory in Cambridge.

q: Which part of the eye controls how much light gets in?
fact: The word 'iris' comes from the Greek for rainbow, a nod to the many different eye colours.

q: Who created the periodic table of elements in 1869?
fact: He left gaps for elements not yet discovered and correctly predicted the properties of gallium and germanium.

q: Which metal is the best conductor of electricity?
fact: Copper is used for most wiring because it conducts almost as well but costs far less.

q: Which part of a cell is often called its 'powerhouse'?
fact: Mitochondria have their own DNA, which is almost always inherited from your mother.

q: Who coined the word 'cell' after looking at cork under a microscope?
fact: He chose the word because the tiny boxes reminded him of the small rooms, or cells, that monks lived in.

q: Which scientist discovered electromagnetic induction in 1831?
fact: Faraday also started the Royal Institution's famous Christmas Lectures for young people, first held in 1825.

q: Which animal is thought to be the longest-living vertebrate?
fact: These sharks grow only about 1 cm a year and are thought not to reach adulthood until around 150 years old.

q: What is a huge, swirling flock of starlings called?
fact: Each starling keeps track of about seven of its neighbours, which lets the whole flock change shape in an instant.

q: Which Australian bird is famous for mimicking sounds like chainsaws and camera shutters?
fact: A male superb lyrebird, with its spectacular tail, appears on the Australian ten-cent coin.

q: Komodo dragons are found in the wild in which country?
fact: In 2006 a female Komodo dragon at Chester Zoo laid fertile eggs without ever having met a male.

q: What colour is the 'sweat' that hippos produce?
fact: The pigments act as a natural sunscreen and also slow the growth of some bacteria on the hippo's skin.

q: Which animal has fingerprints that are almost impossible to tell apart from a human's?
fact: Koalas live almost entirely on eucalyptus leaves, which are toxic to most other animals.

q: Which bird makes the longest known migration of any animal?
fact: Over its lifetime an Arctic tern can fly a distance equal to about three return trips to the Moon.

q: What is the largest animal known to have ever lived?
fact: On a deep dive, a blue whale's heart can slow to just two beats per minute.

q: Which tree gives us conkers?
fact: Although it's a British favourite, the horse chestnut is native to the Balkans and arrived in the UK in the late 1500s.

q: How many sides or points does a typical snowflake have?
fact: In 1885 Vermont farmer Wilson Bentley took the first known photo of a snowflake, and went on to capture over 5,000.

q: How many hearts does an octopus have?
fact: Octopus blood is blue because it carries oxygen using a copper-based molecule instead of iron.

q: Which is the only mammal capable of true powered flight?
fact: Bats aren't actually blind: many see quite well, but they use echolocation to hunt in the dark.

q: Which is the largest living bird?
fact: An ostrich's eye is bigger than its brain.

q: Which tree's spinning seeds are often called 'helicopters'?
fact: The spinning slows the seed's fall, giving the wind more time to carry it away from the parent tree.

q: What is the long, coiled mouthpart a butterfly uses to drink nectar?
fact: Butterflies taste with sensors on their feet, so they can tell if a leaf is good for their eggs just by landing on it.

q: Which scale measures wind strength from 0 for calm to 12 for hurricane force?
fact: It is named after Francis Beaufort, a Royal Navy officer who devised it in 1805 to describe conditions at sea.

q: Which type of cloud is the towering thundercloud?
fact: Their tops can climb more than 10 km high, where they often spread out into a flat 'anvil' shape.

q: Which plant is famous for being one of the fastest-growing on Earth?
fact: Bamboo might look like a tree, but it is actually a type of grass.

q: Which is the only continent with no native ants?
fact: The biggest animal living permanently on land in Antarctica is a wingless midge just a few millimetres long.

q: Which native British tree can live for thousands of years and is often found in churchyards?
fact: Almost every part of the yew is poisonous, except for the soft red flesh around its seeds.

q: What is a baby swan called?
fact: Mute swans aren't really silent: they hiss and snort, and their wings make a loud throbbing sound in flight.

q: What colour is a polar bear's skin under its fur?
fact: Polar bear fur isn't truly white either: each hair is transparent and simply scatters light.

q: Which flightless bird is a national symbol of New Zealand?
fact: A kiwi's egg is enormous for its size, weighing up to about a fifth of the mother's body weight.

q: What type of animal is a slow worm?
fact: Unlike snakes, slow worms can blink, and they can shed their tails to escape from predators.

q: Which of these mammals lays eggs?
fact: Male platypuses have venomous spurs on their back legs, which is very rare among mammals.

q: What is the largest species of penguin?
fact: Male emperor penguins keep the egg warm on their feet through the Antarctic winter, going without food for months.

q: What is the name for a baby hare?
fact: Unlike baby rabbits, young hares are born with fur and open eyes, and can move about within hours.

q: A drey is the nest of which animal?
fact: Like all rodents, squirrels have front teeth that never stop growing, so gnawing keeps them in shape.

q: The name of which seasonal wind comes from the Arabic word for 'season'?
fact: The summer monsoon brings India around three-quarters of its yearly rainfall, all within about four months from June to September.

q: What is a group of lions called?
fact: In a pride, it's usually the lionesses who do most of the hunting, often working together as a team.

q: Which country is the home of paella?
fact: Traditional Valencian paella is made with chicken, rabbit and green beans rather than seafood.

q: Which spice is made from the dried stigmas of a crocus flower?
fact: It takes roughly 150 crocus flowers, all picked by hand, to produce a single gram of saffron.

q: The margherita pizza is famously linked to which Italian city?
fact: Its tomato, mozzarella and basil are said to echo the red, white and green of the Italian flag.

q: Halloumi cheese originally comes from which island?
fact: Halloumi has such a high melting point that it can be grilled or fried without turning runny.

q: Which nut is ground to make marzipan?
fact: The German city of Lübeck is so famous for marzipan that 'Lübecker Marzipan' has protected status in the EU.

q: Earl Grey tea gets its distinctive flavour from which citrus fruit?
fact: Most of the world's bergamot oranges are grown along a small stretch of coast in Calabria, southern Italy.

q: Wasabi belongs to the same plant family as which of these?
fact: Much of the 'wasabi' served outside Japan is actually horseradish dyed green, as real wasabi is costly to grow.

q: Kimchi is a staple of which country's cuisine?
fact: Kimjang, the tradition of families gathering to make kimchi for winter, is on UNESCO's cultural heritage list.

q: Which fruit is the star of a classic tarte Tatin?
fact: The upside-down tart is named after the Tatin sisters, who ran a hotel in Lamotte-Beuvron in France.

q: Feta cheese comes from which country?
fact: To be called feta in the EU, the cheese must be made from sheep's milk, or sheep's milk with up to 30% goat's milk.

q: What is the main ingredient of hummus?
fact: 'Hummus' is simply the Arabic word for chickpea.

q: The croissant is thought to descend from the kipferl, a pastry from which country?
fact: French bakers still call croissants and other buttery pastries 'viennoiseries', a nod to Vienna.

q: Haggis is traditionally cooked inside what?
fact: Haggis takes centre stage at Burns Night suppers on 25 January, served with neeps and tatties.

q: Borscht gets its deep red colour from which vegetable?
fact: Beetroot's red pigment, betanin, is also used as a food colouring with the code E162.

q: Which spirit is made from the blue agave plant?
fact: Tequila takes its name from the town of Tequila in the Mexican state of Jalisco.

q: What does the Italian cooking term 'al dente' literally mean?
fact: Pasta cooked al dente has a lower glycaemic index than overcooked pasta, so its sugars are released more slowly.

q: The mojito cocktail comes from which country?
fact: The daiquiri, another Cuban classic, is named after a beach and an iron mine near Santiago de Cuba.

q: What kind of food is Stinking Bishop?
fact: Its rind is washed in perry made from a pear variety that is also called Stinking Bishop.

q: Which spice gives many curries their golden-yellow colour?
fact: Turmeric's colour comes from curcumin, which is also used as a food colouring with the code E100.

q: Poutine, a dish of chips, cheese curds and gravy, comes from which country?
fact: Poutine first appeared in rural Quebec in the 1950s, and the cheese curds are meant to squeak when you bite them.

q: The pavlova dessert is named after a famous what?
fact: It honours the Russian dancer Anna Pavlova, and both Australia and New Zealand claim to have invented it.

q: Which fruit is used to make the French liqueur crème de cassis?
fact: Mix it with white wine and you get a kir, named after Félix Kir, a former mayor of Dijon.

q: Which noodle soup, pronounced roughly 'fuh', is a Vietnamese classic?
fact: Pho first appeared in northern Vietnam in the early 20th century, around Hanoi and Nam Định.

q: The spice mace comes from the same fruit as which other spice?
fact: Mace is the lacy red covering wrapped around the nutmeg seed, and it turns orange as it dries.

q: The name of the Italian dessert tiramisu translates as what?
fact: Tiramisu is built from coffee-soaked ladyfinger biscuits layered with mascarpone cream.

q: The smörgåsbord buffet comes from which country?
fact: The word combines 'smörgås', meaning open sandwich, and 'bord', meaning table.

q: Which paprika-spiced stew is a national dish of Hungary?
fact: Goulash takes its name from 'gulyás', the Hungarian word for a cattle herdsman.

q: Authentic mozzarella di bufala is made from the milk of which animal?
fact: The name mozzarella comes from 'mozzare', Italian for 'to cut off', describing how the curd is shaped.

q: The coffee plant Coffea arabica is originally native to which country?
fact: The Yemeni port of Mocha, once a major coffee-trading hub, gave its name to the mocha drink.

q: What is the main ingredient of the dip baba ganoush?
fact: Botanically speaking, an aubergine is a berry.

q: Apart from potato, which vegetable is the key ingredient in vichyssoise?
fact: Despite its French name, the chilled soup was popularised by chef Louis Diat at the Ritz-Carlton in New York.

q: Which Mexican sauce often combines chillies with chocolate?
fact: Mole poblano, from the city of Puebla, can contain more than 20 ingredients.

q: Legend says William Webb Ellis invented which sport by running with the ball in 1823?
fact: The trophy for the men's Rugby World Cup is called the Webb Ellis Cup in his honour.

q: The term 'hat-trick' was first used in which sport?
fact: In 1858 bowler H. H. Stephenson took three wickets in three balls in Sheffield, and fans bought him a hat.

q: In which sport might you perform a Salchow?
fact: The jump is named after Swedish skater Ulrich Salchow, who first landed it in competition in 1909.

q: In chess, which piece can only ever move diagonally?
fact: Because it only moves diagonally, a bishop stays on squares of the same colour for the whole game.

q: In tennis, what is a score of zero called?
fact: One popular theory says the 15, 30, 40 scoring came from quarter-hour marks on a clock face.

q: In snooker, how many points is the black ball worth?
fact: A maximum break, potting all 15 reds with a black each followed by every colour, scores 147.

q: Cricket's Ashes series is contested between England and which country?
fact: The Ashes began with a mock obituary in 1882 declaring English cricket dead after a defeat at the Oval.

q: Which country hosted the first FIFA World Cup in 1930?
fact: The hosts also won it, beating Argentina 4–2 in the final in Montevideo.

q: What is the official distance of a marathon?
fact: The odd distance comes from the 1908 London Olympics, whose course ran from Windsor Castle to the stadium.

q: The Stanley Cup is the famous trophy of which sport?
fact: It is named after Lord Stanley of Preston, a Governor General of Canada, who donated it in 1892.

q: What colour jersey does the overall leader wear in the Tour de France?
fact: Yellow was chosen because L'Auto, the newspaper that founded the race in 1903, was printed on yellow paper.

q: Which is the most expensive property on the classic UK Monopoly board?
fact: Monopoly grew out of The Landlord's Game, which Elizabeth Magie patented in 1904.

q: In which sport do players slide stones across ice while teammates sweep?
fact: Many Olympic curling stones are carved from granite quarried on Ailsa Craig, a tiny island off Scotland.

q: Foil, épée and sabre are the three weapons of which sport?
fact: Fencing is one of only a handful of sports to have featured at every modern Olympic Games since 1896.

q: What do all the dots on a standard six-sided dice add up to?
fact: On a standard dice, the numbers on opposite faces always add up to seven.

q: Which martial art's name means 'empty hand'?
fact: Karate developed on the island of Okinawa, in what is now southern Japan.

q: Who was the first person to run a mile in under four minutes?
fact: He clocked 3 minutes 59.4 seconds at Iffley Road in Oxford on 6 May 1954.

q: The 'Fosbury flop' is a technique used in which athletics event?
fact: Dick Fosbury used his backwards technique to win Olympic gold at the 1968 Mexico City Games.

q: How many pieces does each player start with in draughts?
fact: Draughts is played only on the dark squares of the same 8×8 board used for chess.

q: The game Snakes and Ladders originated in which country?
fact: In the original Indian game, the ladders stood for virtues and the snakes for vices.

q: The ancient Olympic Games were held in honour of which Greek god?
fact: By tradition the first recorded Games, in 776 BC, had just one event: a sprint of about 190 metres.

q: In table tennis, a game is normally played up to how many points?
fact: Games used to be played to 21 points until the rules were changed in 2001.

q: The fast stick-and-ball sport of hurling is native to which country?
fact: The women's version of hurling has its own name: camogie.

q: Which sport did astronaut Alan Shepard play on the Moon in 1971?
fact: Shepard's club was a six-iron head fixed to the handle of a tool for collecting lunar samples, folded up to fit on board.

q: The Calcutta Cup is contested by England and Scotland in which sport?
fact: The trophy was made from melted-down silver rupees left over when the Calcutta Football Club closed.

q: Which card game uses a pegboard to keep score?
fact: Cribbage is said to have been devised by the English poet Sir John Suckling in the early 17th century.

q: How long is a cricket pitch from stumps to stumps?
fact: 22 yards is exactly one chain, an old unit that land surveyors used for centuries.

q: Which Jane Austen novel was originally drafted under the title 'First Impressions'?
fact: It was first published anonymously in 1813, credited only to 'the Author of Sense and Sensibility'.

q: Which author created the detective Sherlock Holmes?
fact: Holmes first appeared in A Study in Scarlet in 1887, when Conan Doyle was working as a young doctor.

q: Who wrote the novel Frankenstein?
fact: She began it in 1816 at a villa near Lake Geneva, after Lord Byron challenged his guests to write ghost stories.

q: Which artist painted the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel?
fact: Despite the popular image, he painted it standing up on a scaffold of his own design, not lying on his back.

q: Which Shakespeare play contains the famous 'balcony scene'?
fact: The word 'balcony' never appears in Shakespeare's text: Romeo simply sees Juliet at a window above the orchard.

q: Which Brontë sister wrote Wuthering Heights?
fact: It was first published in 1847 under the male pen name Ellis Bell.

q: Which surrealist painted the melting clocks of 'The Persistence of Memory'?
fact: The famous painting is surprisingly small, measuring only about 24 by 33 centimetres.

q: Who painted 'The Starry Night'?
fact: The painting has belonged to the Museum of Modern Art in New York since 1941.

q: Andy Warhol famously made pop art from cans of which brand of soup?
fact: His 1962 work is made up of 32 separate canvases, one for each variety the company sold at the time.

q: Which composer wrote the set of violin concertos called The Four Seasons?
fact: The concertos were published in 1725 alongside four sonnets describing each season, possibly written by the composer himself.

q: Which composer wrote the music for the ballet The Nutcracker?
fact: He discovered the celesta in Paris and kept it secret so rivals couldn't use its tinkling sound before him.

q: Which silent-film star created the character known as 'The Tramp'?
fact: In 1919 Chaplin co-founded the film studio United Artists with Mary Pickford, Douglas Fairbanks and D. W. Griffith.

q: Which American artist painted 'Nighthawks', showing a late-night diner?
fact: The Art Institute of Chicago bought it for $3,000 within months of its completion in 1942.

q: Winnie-the-Pooh was partly named after a real bear that lived at which zoo?
fact: The bear was called Winnipeg, after the Canadian home city of the soldier who brought her to England.

q: Which composer wrote the orchestral suite The Planets?
fact: He was director of music at St Paul's Girls' School in London from 1905 until his death in 1934.

q: Which composer wrote the Water Music for King George I?
fact: At its 1717 premiere on the Thames, the king reportedly liked it so much that he had it played three times.

q: According to the stories, which country does Paddington Bear come from?
fact: Michael Bond was inspired by a lonely-looking teddy bear he spotted in a London shop on Christmas Eve 1956.

q: Dorothy's magic shoes are silver in the original Oz book. What are they in the 1939 film?
fact: The change was made to show off the bright colours of the then-new Technicolor process.

q: Which Hitchcock film follows a photographer spying on neighbours from his flat?
fact: Hitchcock's cameo in the film shows him winding a clock in a neighbouring songwriter's apartment.

q: Which novel's narrator invites readers to 'Call me Ishmael'?
fact: It sold poorly when published in 1851; its reputation as a masterpiece only grew decades after Melville's death.

q: Which Japanese artist created the woodblock print 'The Great Wave off Kanagawa'?
fact: It is part of his series Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji, and the mountain sits small in the background.

q: In which Italian city can you see Leonardo da Vinci's The Last Supper?
fact: Leonardo painted it on a dry wall rather than as a true fresco, so it began flaking within his lifetime.

q: George Orwell was the pen name of which writer?
fact: Animal Farm was turned down by several publishers before it finally appeared in 1945.

q: Which 1941 film follows newspaper tycoon Charles Foster Kane?
fact: Orson Welles was just 25 when he co-wrote, directed and starred in it.

q: Which composer wrote 'The Blue Danube' waltz?
fact: It was first written in 1867 as a piece for male choir, with words, before becoming famous as an orchestral waltz.

q: What is a word that reads the same backwards as forwards, like 'level', called?
fact: James Joyce's 'tattarrattat', a knock at the door in Ulysses, is often cited as the longest palindromic word in the Oxford English Dictionary.

q: What does the French phrase 'déjà vu' literally mean?
fact: The opposite sensation, when something familiar suddenly feels strangely new, is called 'jamais vu', meaning 'never seen'.

q: The word 'hygge', meaning cosy contentment, is most associated with which country?
fact: It became so popular in Britain that it was shortlisted for Oxford Dictionaries' Word of the Year in 2016.

q: What does the Latin phrase 'carpe diem' mean?
fact: The phrase comes from an ode by the Roman poet Horace, written over 2,000 years ago.

q: Which letter is used most often in written English?
fact: Because it is so common, Morse code gives it the shortest possible signal: a single dot.

q: What is the collective noun for a group of crows?
fact: Many quirky collective nouns come from 15th-century books on hunting and manners, such as the Book of St Albans.

q: Which of these is spelt correctly?
fact: It comes from the Latin 'accommodare', meaning to make fit, which already had the double c and double m.

q: Actors wish each other good luck before a show by saying what?
fact: Saying 'good luck' in a theatre is traditionally thought to bring bad luck.

q: The word 'Schadenfreude', pleasure at someone else's misfortune, comes from which language?
fact: Literally translated, it means something like 'harm-joy'.

q: What is the official language of Brazil?
fact: The explorer Pedro Álvares Cabral claimed Brazil for Portugal in 1500, and it became independent in 1822.

q: What is the term for a word that imitates the sound it describes, like 'buzz'?
fact: Animal noises vary by language: in Japanese, a dog goes 'wan wan'.

q: What do you call a word formed from initial letters and said as a word, like NATO?
fact: 'Scuba' began life as one: self-contained underwater breathing apparatus.

q: What does the German word 'Kindergarten' literally mean?
fact: It was coined in 1840 by the German educator Friedrich Fröbel.

q: The word 'shampoo' comes from which language?
fact: In Regency Brighton, Sake Dean Mahomed ran fashionable 'shampooing' baths offering a kind of Indian therapeutic massage.

q: The word 'bungalow' originally meant a house in the style of which region?
fact: Some of the first houses in England to be called bungalows were built at Westgate-on-Sea in Kent around 1870.

q: The word 'tycoon' entered English from which language?
fact: Abraham Lincoln's secretaries affectionately called him 'the Tycoon'.

q: When it was coined in 1688, what did the word 'nostalgia' describe?
fact: It was invented by Swiss medical student Johannes Hofer from Greek words for 'homecoming' and 'pain'.

q: 'Karaoke' joins the Japanese for 'empty' with a shortened form of which word?
fact: Karaoke machines spread through Japanese bars in the 1970s before the craze went global.

q: The name 'ampersand' comes from children reciting the '&' at the end of what?
fact: The symbol itself started out as the letters e and t joined together, spelling the Latin 'et', meaning 'and'.

q: A sentence that uses every letter of the alphabet is called a what?
fact: A version of 'the quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog' was in print by 1885, recommended for handwriting practice.

q: Which invented language was launched by L. L. Zamenhof in 1887?
fact: Its name comes from Zamenhof's pen name, Doktoro Esperanto, meaning 'one who hopes'.

q: Swapping the first sounds of words, as in 'tease my ears', is named after which Oxford academic?
fact: He was Warden of New College, Oxford, and many of the slips credited to him were probably made up by students.

q: In the NATO phonetic alphabet, which word stands for the letter Q?
fact: 'Alfa' and 'Juliett' are spelt that way so speakers of other languages pronounce them correctly.

q: 'Klutz', 'schmooze' and 'chutzpah' came into English from which language?
fact: It is written in the Hebrew alphabet but is mostly Germanic in its grammar and vocabulary.

q: What is the name for the dot above a lowercase i or j?
fact: The expression 'to a T' may come from the older phrase 'to a tittle'.

q: 'Octothorpe' is another name for which symbol?
fact: Engineers at Bell Labs were using the name by the 1960s for the symbol on new touch-tone telephone keypads.

q: The interrobang punctuation mark combines which two symbols?
fact: It was invented in 1962 by Martin Speckter, an American advertising executive.

q: Which is the hottest planet in our Solar System?
fact: Its thick carbon dioxide atmosphere traps so much heat that the surface is hot enough to melt lead.

q: Who was the first woman to travel into space, in 1963?
fact: On her Vostok 6 flight she orbited Earth 48 times in just under three days.

q: Who became the first human in space in 1961?
fact: His Vostok 1 flight made a single orbit of Earth and lasted about 108 minutes.

q: Which element makes up most of the Sun?
fact: Sunlight takes about eight minutes to travel the 150 million km from the Sun to Earth.

q: Which world was named in 1930 after a suggestion from an 11-year-old Oxford schoolgirl?
fact: Venetia Burney's grandfather, a former head of Oxford's Bodleian Library, passed her idea on to an astronomer friend.

q: Which planet did William Herschel discover from his garden in Bath in 1781?
fact: Herschel wanted to call it Georgium Sidus, meaning 'George's Star', in honour of King George III.

q: What is the largest moon in the Solar System?
fact: Jupiter's moon Ganymede is bigger than the planet Mercury and is the only moon known to have its own magnetic field.

q: Which space telescope, launched in 1990, is named after an American astronomer?
fact: Soon after launch its main mirror was found to be slightly flawed; astronauts fitted corrective optics in 1993.

q: Who became the first Briton in space, in 1991?
fact: She applied after hearing a radio advert that said: 'Astronaut wanted. No experience necessary.'

q: In 2016, astronaut Tim Peake ran which city's marathon on a treadmill aboard the ISS?
fact: Strapped to the treadmill by a harness, he finished in 3 hours, 35 minutes and 21 seconds.

q: Which NASA Mars rover was planned to last 90 days but kept working for almost 15 years?
fact: By the end of its mission it had driven 45.16 km across Mars, further than a marathon.

q: Which Cheshire observatory's giant dish tracked the rocket that launched Sputnik in 1957?
fact: Its 76-metre (250 ft) dish is now called the Lovell Telescope, after the observatory's founder Bernard Lovell.

q: The Plough, also called the Big Dipper, is part of which constellation?
fact: The two stars at the end of the Plough's 'pan' point the way to Polaris, the North Star.

q: What is the name for the huge explosion of a massive star at the end of its life?
fact: The Crab Nebula is the glowing remains of a supernova recorded by Chinese astronomers in 1054.

q: What is the boundary around a black hole beyond which nothing, not even light, can escape?
fact: In 2019 the Event Horizon Telescope revealed the first ever image of a black hole, in the galaxy M87.

q: What name is often given to a second full moon in the same calendar month?
fact: Despite the name it doesn't look blue, and one comes along roughly every two to three years.

q: Which Apollo mission had to abandon its Moon landing after an oxygen tank burst in 1970?
fact: The three astronauts used their lunar module, Aquarius, as a lifeboat to get safely home.

q: Which is the farthest planet from the Sun?
fact: In 1846 Neptune became the first planet found by mathematical prediction rather than by scanning the sky.

q: Which is the brightest star in the night sky?
fact: Sirius is nicknamed the Dog Star because it sits in the constellation Canis Major, the Great Dog.

q: In which constellation would you find the red supergiant Betelgeuse?
fact: Orion's Belt is made up of three bright stars called Alnitak, Alnilam and Mintaka.

q: Which dwarf planet is the largest object in the asteroid belt?
fact: It was first spotted by the astronomer Giuseppe Piazzi in Sicily on New Year's Day, 1801.

q: Which is the only planet in our Solar System not named after a Greek or Roman god?
fact: Earth is also the densest planet in the Solar System, thanks largely to its heavy iron core.

q: What does a light year measure?
fact: One light year is about 9.46 trillion kilometres, the distance light travels in a year.

q: Which astronomer discovered Jupiter's four largest moons in 1610?
fact: He first named them the Medicean Stars, after his powerful patrons, the Medici family of Florence.

q: In 2019, China's Chang'e 4 made the first ever soft landing where?
options: The far side of the Moon
fact: It carried cotton seeds that briefly sprouted, the first seeds ever to germinate on the Moon.

q: What do we call a space rock that survives its fall and lands on Earth?
fact: Most shooting stars are caused by specks of space dust about the size of a grain of sand.

q: Which Scottish city is nicknamed the Granite City?
fact: Thanks to mica in the stone, its buildings can sparkle in the sun, giving it another nickname: the Silver City.

q: What is the largest lake in the UK by surface area?
fact: This Northern Irish lough supplies around 40% of Northern Ireland's drinking water.

q: Which Somerset city is famous for its Royal Crescent and Roman Baths?
fact: About 1.17 million litres of hot spring water, at around 46°C, still rise there every day.

q: At which London landmark is the Ceremony of the Keys held every night?
fact: The ceremony, in which the gates are locked for the night, has taken place for at least 700 years.

q: The Beatles made their name at the Cavern Club in which city?
fact: By one count, the band made 292 appearances at the club between 1961 and 1963.

q: How many passenger capsules does the London Eye have?
fact: The capsules are numbered up to 33, because number 13 is skipped for luck.

q: What is the nickname of the skyscraper at 30 St Mary Axe in the City of London?
fact: Despite its curvy shape, its only curved piece of glass is the lens-shaped cap at the very top.

q: Which Scottish loch holds more water than all the lakes of England and Wales combined?
fact: The famous 1934 'Surgeon's Photograph' of Nessie was later revealed to be a toy submarine with a model head.

q: Which Northern Irish landmark is made of around 40,000 interlocking basalt columns?
fact: Legend says the giant Finn McCool built it as a path across the sea to Scotland.

q: The village with the very long name beginning Llanfairpwllgwyngyll is on which Welsh island?
fact: Its 58-character full name is thought to have been dreamt up in the 1860s as a publicity stunt for the railway station.

q: The Buckinghamshire town of Olney is famous for a race held on which day?
fact: By tradition the pancake race dates back to 1445, and runners must wear an apron and a head covering.

q: Which chocolate-making family built the model village of Bournville near Birmingham?
fact: George Cadbury was a Quaker who opposed alcohol, and no pub has ever been built in Bournville.

q: The 700-year-old Coronation Chair is kept in which London church?
fact: Made for Edward I in 1300-1301, its back is covered in names carved by Westminster schoolboys and visitors in the 1700s and 1800s.

q: At what time is a gun fired from Edinburgh Castle on most days?
fact: First fired in 1861, it allowed ships in the Firth of Forth to set their clocks accurately.

q: Which London department store installed England's first moving staircase in 1898?
fact: Staff waited at the top to offer brandy and smelling salts to shoppers shaken by the ride.

q: In which city did eight uninvited theatre groups start the famous Fringe festival in 1947?
fact: Playwright Robert Kemp coined the name in 1948, writing that 'round the fringe of official Festival drama' there was more private enterprise.

q: What is the highest mountain in the UK?
fact: A weather observatory operated on its summit from 1883 until 1904.

q: Harry Beck's famous diagram, first published in 1933, is a map of what?
fact: Beck ignored real distances, spacing stations evenly and drawing lines only horizontally, vertically or at 45 degrees.

q: Which English cathedral has Britain's tallest cathedral spire, at 123 metres?
fact: It also holds the best preserved of the four surviving original copies of the 1215 Magna Carta.

q: Which Welsh city is often described as the smallest city in Britain?
fact: Legend says Wales's patron saint was born on the nearby clifftops, at a spot now called St Non's.

q: Which London gardens are home to a ten-storey Great Pagoda built in the 1760s?
fact: In 2018, 80 colourful dragons returned to its roofs for the first time since the 1780s.

q: What is the longest river in the UK?
fact: Its tidal surge, the Severn Bore, is a wave that surfers can ride for miles upstream.

q: In 2012, the clock tower at the Houses of Parliament was renamed what?
fact: Big Ben is strictly the name of the tower's great bell, which weighs about 13.7 tonnes.

q: Which London bridge can be raised to let tall ships pass along the Thames?
fact: It opened in 1894, and its huge lifting sections were originally powered by steam engines.

q: In which English county is Stonehenge?
fact: Many of its smaller 'bluestones' were brought about 150 miles from the Preseli Hills in west Wales.

q: What is the national animal of Scotland?
fact: In heraldry, the Scottish unicorn is usually shown wearing a golden chain.

q: Which London railway station gave its name to a famous marmalade-loving bear?
fact: In the original stories, the bear arrives from Peru with a label saying 'Please look after this bear'.

q: Which London Underground line is shown in yellow on the Tube map?
fact: The Metropolitan line, opened in 1863, was the world's first underground railway.

q: Which is the oldest university in the UK?
fact: There is evidence of teaching there by 1096, making it the oldest university in the English-speaking world.

q: On which London street did Sherlock Holmes famously live, at number 221B?
fact: When the stories were written, house numbers on Baker Street did not actually go as high as 221.

q: In Scotland, what is Hogmanay?
fact: In 'first-footing', the first visitor after midnight is said to bring luck, ideally carrying a gift such as coal.

q: What is the name of the imaginary line around the middle of the Earth?
fact: The Equator passes through Brazil, Kenya and Indonesia, among other countries.

q: What is the capital of Russia?
fact: Moscow's metro is famous for grand stations decorated with chandeliers and mosaics.

q: Which is the largest continent?
fact: Around six in every ten people in the world live in Asia.

q: Amsterdam is the capital of which country?
fact: About a quarter of the Netherlands lies below sea level, protected by dykes and dunes.

q: Brussels is the capital of which country?
fact: Belgium has three official languages: Dutch, French and German.

q: Kenya is in which continent?
fact: Kenya takes its name from Mount Kenya, the second-highest mountain in Africa.

q: Hollywood, the home of the US film industry, is in which city?
fact: The famous Hollywood sign originally read 'Hollywoodland' and advertised new houses.

q: Which sea lies between southern Europe and North Africa?
fact: The name 'Mediterranean' comes from Latin words meaning 'in the middle of the land'.

q: Which US state is made up entirely of islands?
fact: Hawaii's islands were formed by volcanoes, and some of those volcanoes are still active.

q: Which famous Paris landmark was built for the World's Fair of 1889?
fact: The Eiffel Tower was originally only meant to stand for 20 years.

q: Who was Queen Elizabeth II's husband?
fact: Elizabeth and Philip married at Westminster Abbey in 1947.

q: Which explorer famously sailed across the Atlantic to the Americas in 1492?
fact: Columbus was born in Genoa, in what is now Italy, but his famous voyage was paid for by Spain.

q: Which country was once ruled by tsars?
fact: The word 'tsar' comes from 'Caesar', the title used by Roman emperors.

q: Steam, or water vapour, is water in which state?
fact: True steam is invisible: the white cloud above a kettle is really tiny water droplets.

q: What is it called when water slowly turns into vapour, like a drying puddle?
fact: Puddles dry up faster on warm, windy days because evaporation speeds up.

q: What does a thermometer measure?
fact: Normal human body temperature is about 37°C.

q: Which organ pumps blood around the body?
fact: An adult heart beats around 100,000 times every day.

q: What does a caterpillar turn into?
fact: Inside its chrysalis, a caterpillar breaks down almost completely before rebuilding itself.

q: Which animal is famous for building dams across rivers?
fact: Beavers have orange teeth, coloured by iron that makes them extra strong.

q: What is a baby goat called?
fact: Goats have rectangular pupils, which give them a very wide field of view.

q: What are small balls of ice that fall from storm clouds called?
fact: Hailstones grow in layers as they're tossed up and down inside storm clouds.

q: Which tall yellow flower is named after the Sun?
fact: Young sunflowers follow the Sun across the sky, but most fully grown ones face east.

q: Which large fruit has a hard, hairy shell and watery juice inside?
fact: Despite its name, a coconut is botanically a drupe rather than a true nut.

q: What is the traditional filling of a Cornish pasty?
fact: Genuine Cornish pasties have protected status and must be prepared in Cornwall.

q: Which vegetable is traditionally carved into a lantern at Halloween?
fact: In Ireland and Scotland, people carved turnips long before pumpkins caught on.

q: In cricket, how many balls are bowled in a standard over?
fact: An over in which the bowler gives away no runs is called a maiden.

q: In darts, what is the highest score possible with three darts?
fact: A 180 needs all three darts to land in the treble 20, the thin inner ring worth triple points.

q: In boxing, what does KO stand for?
fact: Despite being called a ring, a boxing ring is actually square.

q: In which sport would you perform on a balance beam?
fact: The balance beam used in gymnastics is just 10 centimetres wide.

q: Which sport is played at Wimbledon?
fact: Players at Wimbledon must wear almost entirely white clothing.

q: The Grand National is a famous event in which sport?
fact: The Grand National is held at Aintree Racecourse, near Liverpool.

q: What is the official in charge of a football match called?
fact: The assistant referees who run the touchlines used to be called linesmen.

q: What shape is a rugby ball?
fact: Early rugby balls were made from pigs' bladders covered in leather.

q: What is the name of the young lion in The Lion King?
fact: 'Simba' is the Swahili word for 'lion'.

q: What colour do you get by mixing blue and yellow paint?
fact: Painters have traditionally been taught that red, yellow and blue are the three primary colours.

q: Which author wrote the Famous Five books?
fact: Enid Blyton was incredibly productive and wrote hundreds of books during her career.

q: Which musical instrument usually has 88 black and white keys?
fact: The piano's full name, 'pianoforte', means 'soft-loud' in Italian.

q: How many dwarfs does Snow White meet in the Disney film?
fact: Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs (1937) was Disney's first full-length animated feature film.

q: Which fictional spy is known by the code number 007?
fact: Ian Fleming borrowed the name James Bond from an American expert on birds.

q: Which superhero is secretly Peter Parker?
fact: Spider-Man first swung into comics in 1962, in an issue of Amazing Fantasy.

q: In which town was William Shakespeare born?
fact: You can still visit the house on Henley Street where Shakespeare is believed to have been born.

q: In The Jungle Book, what kind of animal is Baloo?
fact: The Jungle Book stories were written by Rudyard Kipling and first published in 1894.

q: What is the famous nickname of the Academy Award statuette?
fact: Each Oscar statuette is made of bronze and plated in 24-carat gold.

q: How many letters are in the English alphabet?
fact: Words now spelt with a J, like 'jest', were once often written with an I instead.

q: What do you call a word that means the same as another word?
fact: A thesaurus is a book of synonyms, and its name comes from a Greek word for 'treasure house'.

q: 'Listen' and 'silent' use the same letters. What is this called?
fact: With a little rearranging, the letters of 'dormitory' spell 'dirty room'.

q: What are words like 'sea' and 'see', which sound the same but mean different things?
fact: 'Homophone' comes from the Greek for 'same sound'.

q: What does BBC stand for?
fact: The BBC began life in 1922 as the British Broadcasting Company, before becoming a corporation.

q: What do you call a word like 'he', 'she' or 'they' that stands in for a noun?
fact: Words like 'and', 'but' and 'or', which join parts of a sentence, are called conjunctions.

q: What does 'e.g.' mean?
fact: 'e.g.' is short for the Latin 'exempli gratia', meaning 'for the sake of example'.

q: What word describes someone who speaks two languages fluently?
fact: 'Bilingual' comes from the Latin 'bi' (two) and 'lingua', meaning tongue.

q: What does ISS stand for in space travel?
fact: The International Space Station zooms all the way around Earth roughly every 90 minutes.

q: What is it called when the Moon blocks our view of the Sun during the day?
fact: The Sun is about 400 times wider than the Moon but also about 400 times farther away, so they look the same size.

q: What is the Moon mainly made of?
fact: Many scientists think the Moon formed from debris after a Mars-sized object hit the young Earth.

q: What are the rocky objects that mostly orbit the Sun between Mars and Jupiter?
fact: Some asteroids even have their own tiny moons orbiting them.

q: What is the name for the thin, curved shape the Moon sometimes appears as?
fact: Sunlight bounced off Earth, called earthshine, can make the dark part of a crescent moon faintly glow.

q: What name is given to the Sun and all the planets that travel around it?
fact: 'Solar' comes from 'sol', the Latin word for the Sun.

q: Roughly how long does it take Earth to spin once on its axis?
fact: Earth's spin is very gradually slowing down, so days were shorter when dinosaurs lived.

q: What do we call a group of stars that forms a pattern or picture in the sky?
fact: Astronomers officially recognise 88 constellations covering the whole sky.

q: What is the name for the path one object takes around another in space?
fact: Planets' orbits are not perfect circles but slightly squashed ovals called ellipses.

q: Which prickly purple flower is the national emblem of Scotland?
fact: A thistle appears on the badge of Scotland's national rugby team.

q: The bell known as Big Ben hangs in a tower at which London building?
fact: Big Ben weighs more than 13 tonnes and began striking the hours in 1859.

q: The famous White Cliffs stand beside which Kent port?
fact: The White Cliffs are made of chalk, formed from the remains of tiny sea creatures.

q: Which northern English city is home to both United and City football clubs?
fact: Manchester's symbol, the worker bee, celebrates the city's busy industrial past.
